overview.title: Evaluating on the test set, overfitting, and what a tensor is
overview.chapter: 2 The mathematical building blocks of neural networks
overview.main_topic: Closing the first MNIST example (argmax of a prediction, checking the label, `model.evaluate()` giving 97.8 % test accuracy, the training/test gap named overfitting), then opening section 2.2 with the definition of a tensor as a container for numbers generalizing matrices to any number of axes.
overview.central_idea: A model's real quality is its accuracy on data it never saw; the gap between 98.9 % training and 97.8 % test accuracy is overfitting. All the data flowing through such a model is stored in tensors, multidimensional arrays that generalize matrices.
overview.importance: The page delivers the first measurement of generalization in the book and names the central problem of machine learning (overfitting, chapter 5). It also pivots from 'look at an example' to 'understand the pieces', starting with tensors, the data structure every later chapter manipulates.
learning_objectives: Turn a softmax probability vector into a predicted class with `argmax()` and verify it against the true label.
Use `model.evaluate()` to obtain test loss and test accuracy over the whole test set.
Explain why a training/test accuracy gap is called overfitting and why the test number is the one that matters.
Define a tensor as a container for (usually numerical) data that generalizes matrices to an arbitrary number of axes.
prerequisites: Training accuracy 0.989 reported by `fit()` on p.44.
Familiarity with matrices as grids of numbers; NumPy arrays from p.42.

summary:
The page completes the first example. `predictions[0].argmax()` returns 7 and `predictions[0][7]` is 0.99999106; `test_labels[0]` is also 7, so the prediction for the first test digit is correct.

To measure how good the model is on average over *never-before-seen* digits, **Listing 2.7** calls `model.evaluate(test_images, test_labels)`, which returns the test loss and test accuracy; the accuracy prints as `0.9785`. The authors point out that 97.8 % on the test set is *almost double the error rate* of the training set (98.9 % accuracy, i.e. 1.1 % error vs 2.2 %). This gap is an example of **overfitting**: machine learning models tend to perform worse on new data than on their training data. Overfitting is a central topic of chapter 5.

This concludes the first example: a neural network that classifies handwritten digits in fewer than 15 lines of Python. The rest of this chapter and the next will explain every moving piece: **tensors** (the data-storing objects that go into the model), **tensor operations** (what layers are made of), and **gradient descent** (how the model learns from training examples).

Section **2.2, Data representations for neural networks**, begins. The MNIST example started from multidimensional NumPy arrays, also called *tensors*; all current machine learning systems use tensors as their basic data structure, so fundamental that TensorFlow is named after them. A tensor is, at its core, a container for data, usually numerical data: a container for numbers. Matrices are rank-2 tensors; tensors generalize matrices to an arbitrary number of dimensions, where in tensor language a dimension is usually called an *axis*. The details may look abstract, but manipulating tensors will be the bread and butter of any machine learning code the reader writes.

concepts.name: Overfitting
concepts.definition: The fact that machine learning models tend to perform worse on new data than on their training data.
concepts.intuition: A student who memorizes last year's exam scores 99 % on it but only 98 % on a fresh exam; the drop is what was memorized rather than understood.
concepts.technical: Observed as a gap between training accuracy (98.9 %) and test accuracy (97.8 %), equivalently an error rate that doubles from 1.1 % to 2.2 %. Chapter 5 explains it in terms of model capacity, data size and regularization.
concepts.significance: The authors call it a central topic of chapter 5; it is the main reason test and validation sets exist.
concepts.example: Listing 2.7: `test_acc: 0.9785` versus 0.989 on the training data.
concepts.misconception: Overfitting does not mean the model is bad in absolute terms; 97.8 % is excellent. It means the training number overstates true performance.

concepts.name: evaluate()
concepts.definition: The Keras method that computes a model's loss and metrics over a dataset of inputs and targets.
concepts.intuition: Grade the model on the exam it has never seen and report the average score.
concepts.technical: `model.evaluate(x, y)` runs the forward pass on all samples (no weight updates) and returns `[loss, metric1, ...]` as configured in `compile()`; here `(test_loss, test_acc)`.
concepts.significance: Provides the honest, held-out estimate of performance that the training log cannot.
concepts.misconception: `evaluate()` is not `predict()`: it returns aggregate scores, not per-sample outputs.

concepts.name: argmax decision rule
concepts.definition: Choosing the class with the largest predicted probability.
concepts.intuition: Pick the digit the model is most confident about.
concepts.technical: `predictions[0].argmax()` returns the index of the maximum entry (7); `predictions[0][7]` is that maximum, 0.99999106.
concepts.significance: It is how a probabilistic classifier produces a hard label, and how accuracy is computed.
concepts.misconception: argmax discards the confidence; two predictions with probabilities 0.51 and 0.999 produce the same label.

concepts.name: Tensor
concepts.definition: A container for data, usually numerical: a generalization of matrices to an arbitrary number of dimensions (axes).
concepts.intuition: A number is a point, a list of numbers a line, a grid a sheet, a stack of grids a block; a tensor is this idea continued to any number of index directions.
concepts.technical: Characterized by rank (number of axes), shape (size along each axis) and dtype (p.47). NumPy `ndarray`s, and the tensors of TensorFlow, PyTorch and JAX, implement it.
concepts.significance: The basic data structure of all current machine learning systems; inputs, targets, weights and gradients are all tensors.
concepts.example: The MNIST training images: rank-3 tensor of shape (60000, 28, 28), reshaped to rank 2 (60000, 784).
concepts.misconception: In machine learning 'tensor' just means multidimensional array; it does not carry the transformation laws of the physics/geometry notion.

concepts.name: Rank and axes
concepts.definition: The rank of a tensor is its number of axes; an axis is what is often called a dimension in tensor context.
concepts.intuition: How many indices you need to name one element: 0 for a scalar, 2 for a matrix, 3 for a stack of images.
concepts.technical: NumPy exposes it as `ndim`. Matrices are rank-2; rank-n tensors have n axes.
concepts.significance: Rank determines what operations apply and how layers interpret data (p.50: vectors, time series, images, video each have a characteristic rank).
concepts.example: A matrix such as a (60000, 784) array has rank 2 and two axes: samples and features.
concepts.misconception: 'Dimension' is ambiguous: a 5D vector has one axis with 5 entries, while a 5D tensor has five axes (p.46).

math.title: Accuracy and error rate on the test set

Fraction of the 10,000 test images classified correctly.

math.operations: For each test sample take the argmax of the prediction, compare with the label, count the matches, divide by the number of samples.
math.purpose: Quantify generalization: performance on data the model never trained on.
math.interpretation: 9,785 of 10,000 test digits are right. The error rates are 1 - 0.989 = 1.1 % (train) and 1 - 0.9785 = 2.15 % (test): the test error is almost double, which is the authors' 'almost double the error rate'.
math.intuition: Accuracies 98.9 and 97.8 look close; error rates 1.1 and 2.2 make the gap obvious. Thinking in errors magnifies what matters.
math.numerical_example: Train: 0.011 x 60000 ≈ 660 misclassified training images. Test: 0.0215 x 10000 = 215 misclassified test images, out of a set six times smaller.

code.title: Evaluating the model on new data
code.original_code:
>>> test_loss, test_acc = model.evaluate(test_images, test_labels)
>>> print(f"test_acc: {test_acc}")
test_acc: 0.9785
code.what_it_does: Computes the average loss and accuracy of the trained model over all 10,000 test images and prints the accuracy, 0.9785.

line_explanations.explanation: `evaluate()` runs inference over the test set in batches and returns the loss and every metric from `compile()`, unpacked here into `test_loss` and `test_acc`.
Prints the accuracy with an f-string: 97.85 % of test digits are classified correctly.

code.inputs_outputs: In: `test_images` (10000, 784) float32, `test_labels` (10000,). Out: two floats; the weights are untouched.
code.algorithm: Forward pass on each batch, sparse categorical cross-entropy and accuracy accumulated, then averaged.
code.theory_link: This measures generalization and exposes the overfitting gap discussed in the next paragraph.

parameters.role: Inputs the model never saw during training.

parameters.name: test_labels

pitfalls: The order of returned values follows `compile()`: loss first, then metrics in the order given.
Evaluating repeatedly on the test set while tuning the model turns it into a validation set and makes the final estimate optimistic (chapter 5 discusses this).
code.illustrative_code:
# AI-written: compute the same accuracy by hand from predict()
import numpy as np
all_preds = model.predict(test_images).argmax(axis=1)
print((all_preds == test_labels).mean())   # ~0.9785
print("train error %.3f, test error %.3f" % (1 - 0.989, 1 - 0.9785))

deeper.title: Why the authors talk about error rate instead of accuracy
deeper.body:
The page says 97.8 % is 'almost double the error rate' of 98.9 %. The arithmetic:

- training error = 100 - 98.9 = **1.1 %**
- test error = 100 - 97.85 = **2.15 %**
- ratio = 2.15 / 1.1 ≈ **1.95**

Expressed as accuracies the difference is a modest 1.1 percentage points; expressed as errors the model makes nearly twice as many mistakes on new digits. Beyond the book: this framing is standard practice when accuracies are high, because the error is what a user experiences (one mistake in 46 digits instead of one in 91), and improvements are naturally measured as relative reductions of error.

deeper.title: The model as an over-eager student
deeper.body: Think of the 60,000 training digits as a practice workbook and the 10,000 test digits as the final exam. After five passes through the workbook, the student gets 98.9 % of the workbook right. On the exam, 97.8 %. Part of the workbook score came from recognizing *those specific pages*: a smudge here, an unusually slanted 7 there, cues that will never recur on the exam. That memorized part is the overfitting. The goal of chapter 5 is to make the workbook score a faithful predictor of the exam score, usually by making the student rely on general shape rather than page-specific quirks.

deeper.title: From the example to the chapter's three themes
deeper.body:
The closing paragraph names three things to be explained; here is where each was already silently used in Listings 2.1-2.7:

| Theme | Where it appeared in the example | Where it is explained |
|---|---|---|
| Tensors (data-storing objects going into the model) | `train_images` of shape (60000, 28, 28) -> (60000, 784), `test_labels` of shape (10000,) | Section 2.2, p.45-51 |
| Tensor operations (what layers are made of) | each `Dense` layer's `relu(dot(input, W) + b)`; the `/ 255` rescaling; `reshape` | Section 2.3, p.52-62 |
| Gradient descent (how the model learns) | everything inside `model.fit(...)`: 2,345 weight updates driven by the loss | Section 2.4, p.63-74 |

Section 2.5 (p.75-82) then rebuilds the whole example from scratch using only these three ingredients.

visualizations.why: Shows the numbers on this page side by side: 98.9 % vs 97.85 % accuracy looks small, but 1.1 % vs 2.15 % error makes the 'almost double' claim visible.

visualizations.why: Section 2.2 defines a tensor as a generalization of matrices to any number of axes. These are the actual tensors the example used, from rank-3 image stacks down to rank-1 labels and rank-2 predictions.

misconceptions.claim: A 1.1-point drop from training to test accuracy is negligible, so there is no overfitting.
misconceptions.correction: The authors measure the gap in error rate, which nearly doubles (1.1 % to 2.15 %). Any systematic train/test gap is overfitting; its size, not its existence, is what regularization techniques in chapter 5 reduce.

misconceptions.claim: `model.evaluate()` trains the model a little on the test data.
misconceptions.correction: `evaluate()` only runs forward passes and aggregates loss and metrics; the weights are not modified.

misconceptions.claim: A tensor is just a fancy word for a matrix.
misconceptions.correction: A matrix is the special case of rank 2. Tensors have any number of axes: the MNIST image stack is rank 3, and p.50 shows rank-4 and rank-5 data tensors.

misconceptions.claim: Since `predictions[0][7]` is 0.99999106, the model is 99.999 % likely to be right on this digit.
misconceptions.correction: Softmax outputs express the model's confidence, which is not a calibrated guarantee; over the whole test set the model is wrong 2.15 % of the time, and some of those errors will be confident ones.

questions.question: What does `model.evaluate(test_images, test_labels)` return in Listing 2.7?
options: The predicted class for every test image
The test loss and the test accuracy
The updated weights after training on the test set
questions.answer: The test loss and the test accuracy
questions.explanation: The listing unpacks the result into `test_loss, test_acc`: the compiled loss and the `accuracy` metric averaged over the test set. Per-image predictions come from `predict()` (p.44); `evaluate()` never updates weights.

questions.question: Training accuracy is 98.9 % and test accuracy 97.85 %. Compute both error rates and explain the authors' phrase 'almost double the error rate'.
questions.answer: Training error 1.1 %, test error 2.15 %; 2.15 / 1.1 ≈ 1.95, so the test error is almost twice the training error.
questions.explanation: Error rate = 1 - accuracy. A 1.1-point accuracy gap corresponds to nearly doubling the fraction of mistakes, which is why the authors express the gap in error terms.

questions.question: Define overfitting as the page does, and explain why it can only be detected by evaluating on data outside the training set.
questions.answer: Overfitting is the tendency of models to perform worse on new data than on their training data. Training accuracy alone cannot reveal it because it measures performance on the very data the model adapted to; only a held-out set shows the drop.
questions.explanation: The page defines overfitting as 'the fact that machine learning models tend to perform worse on new data than on their training data' and discovers it precisely by comparing `fit()`'s training accuracy with `evaluate()`'s test accuracy.

questions.question: According to section 2.2, what is a tensor?
options: A container for numerical data generalizing matrices to any number of axes
A synonym for a two-dimensional matrix
A Keras layer that stores weights
A TensorFlow-specific data type unavailable in NumPy
questions.answer: A container for numerical data generalizing matrices to any number of axes
questions.explanation: The page says a tensor is 'a container for data—usually numerical data' and that 'tensors are a generalization of matrices to an arbitrary number of dimensions'. Matrices are only the rank-2 case; layers are built *from* tensor operations; NumPy arrays are tensors too.

questions.question: Why do the authors prefer the word 'axis' to 'dimension' when talking about tensors?
questions.answer: Because 'dimension' is ambiguous in tensor context: it can mean the number of axes or the number of entries along an axis; 'axis' unambiguously means an index direction of the tensor.
questions.explanation: The page notes that 'in the context of tensors, a dimension is often called an axis'; p.46 spells out the 5D-vector vs 5D-tensor confusion that motivates this.

questions.question: Name the three topics the authors say the rest of this chapter and the next will explain, and what each corresponds to in the example.
questions.answer: Tensors (the data-storing objects going into the model), tensor operations (which layers are made of), and gradient descent (which lets the model learn from its training examples).
questions.explanation: This is the road map in the closing paragraph of section 2.1; sections 2.2, 2.3 and 2.4 cover them in that order.

questions.question: Can you explain, without notes, why 9,785 correct test digits out of 10,000 is a more trustworthy number than the 98.9 % printed during training?
questions.answer: The test digits were never used to adjust the weights, so their accuracy estimates performance on genuinely new data; the training accuracy is inflated by overfitting.
questions.explanation: Self-assessment on the central lesson of the page. If unsure, reread the overfitting paragraph and the analogy in the Deeper section.
